title: How to Compose a Gat
summary: How to compose a gat: set the rāga's main note on sam with a pause, move toward the saṃvādī, rest on Sa, fill the remaining beats, and start playing from the phrase leading into sam. Bhūpālī examples in Rūpak and Tīntāl follow, then ornamenting, śruti defined, and the kinds and making of tihāīs.

prev.title: Here Begins the Section on Performance

blocks.text: Method of composing a gat (gat nirmāṇa)
Now, having understood the importance of sam, nyāsa, tāla and words, we must move on to composing a gat or gīt. On this subject the following methods are described.

blocks.verse:
रागांगस्तु समे स्थाप्यो विरामस्तत्र शोभते।
राग वाचिक्रमेणैव ततः संवादिनं ब्रजेत।१३६।
blocks.text: The rāga's main part should be placed on the sam, and a pause there is graceful; then, following the order of the rāga's identifying notes, one should move to the saṃvādī.

That is, for any rāga whose gat (instrumental composition) is to be made, write its note against the first mātrā (beat) of the chosen tāla, and put a pause mark (–) of at least one mātrā on the second mātrā. After that, keeping in mind the movement of that rāga, move towards the saṃvādī (consonant second note) as an apanyāsa (intermediate resting note), and whatever notes you think proper to use in it, count them and write them under the remaining mātrās. Then, moving on from there, make a nyāsa (resting note) on Sa with a pause of at least one mātrā. Write the notes of that nyāsa, in turn, under the remaining mātrās. Now, if the mātrās of the tāla have not all been filled, count those remaining mātrās and devise a group of notes of that many mātrās which can make a nyāsa on the vādī (principal note) placed earlier. Now, when playing it, do not begin from the first mātrā but from that very group of notes devised as the nyāsa of the vādī note. Just as, when making a bansī, the order of marking the svarasthānas (note positions) is one thing and the order of making holes at those marks is another, in the same way the order of notes when composing a gat differs from the order of notes when playing it. For example, if Rāga Bhūpālī is to be set in Rūpak tāla, then after writing the number of mātrās of the tāla, with its division of mātrās, properly in the form of a grid, the notes of Bhūpālī will be entered against those very signs by the method given above. In the grid below, the numbers at the top are in the order of the tāla, and the composing has also been done in that order. That note will not be played at the beginning when playing. But sometimes, as an exception, the order of composing and the order of playing remain the same.
To complete the methods given above, there are also the following ślokas

blocks.verse:
बहुत्वाल्पत्वनिर्वाहपुर्वकम् षड्जम् न्यसेत्।
कालमानानुसारेण स्वारावृत्तिम् सृजेत् क्वचित्।१३७।
blocks.text: Observing which notes are frequent and which sparing, one should make the nyāsa on Ṣaḍja; and now and then, according to the measure of time, one may create repetition of notes.

That is, whatever note the nyāsa is on, sometimes while making the nyāsa a problem arises when the notes come to more than the regular mātrās of the tāla, or when the number of notes falls short of the tāla's mātrās. To solve that problem the number of notes has to be reduced or increased. Then, according to the śāstra, one should increase the count of whichever note has more importance in the rāga, and reduce the count of the note whose importance is less. Besides this, another way is to join a note of alpatva (sparing use) with a neighbouring note and put both in double speed within one mātrā, or to give a pause of one mātrā on a note of bahutva (frequent use). Doing this makes it easy to weigh the rāga into the tāla. This method has been used in the following gat.

The gat above has also been composed by the method given earlier. While composing, the nyāsa was kept in mind from the first mātrā to the sixteenth, but in use, for the sake of beauty, it was begun from the twelfth mātrā itself and one āvartan (cycle) was taken to run up to the eleventh mātrā. In the same way gats can be made and played by the method given above in many tālas, such as Jhaptāl. Now, after a gat has been composed, if a poem of the same number of mātrās is fitted into that gat, it can become a song and a subject for singing. Some people do just this. It makes it even easier for them to remember the gat. The method by which these should be made pleasing to the ear is described in the next śloka.

blocks.verse:
श्रुतिस्पर्शैः स्वरस्पर्शैः कम्पनैः भूषयेत् स्वरान्।
श्रवणेन परीक्ष्यैनम् तालेन परिशोधयेत्।१३८।
blocks.text: One should adorn the notes with touches of śruti, touches of other notes and shakes; testing it by ear, one should refine it with the tāla.

That is, one should try to make the notes used in a song sweet by joining them sometimes with the touch of a śruti (mīṇḍ, glide), with the touch of other notes, and with actions such as kampana (shake). For the definition of śruti, here is the following śloka.

blocks.verse:
स्वराणामन्तराले च सन्ति नादा अनेकाशः।
श्रूयते तत्र यो भिन्नः स नादः श्रुति संज्ञकः।१३९।
blocks.text: In the spaces between the notes there are many sounds; the one among them that is heard as distinct is the sound called śruti.

Although in the śāstra of music differing views are found on whether the śrutis are equal or unequal, yet on this matter all are of one opinion: among the many sounds (nāda) lying in the space between the notes, those whose difference, though subtle, can be heard are called śrutis. [Still finer] intervals of sound, in number [beyond these], can also be seen by means of instruments, but we cannot give them the name śruti, because those differences depend on instruments - human life cannot always rely on these instruments.

blocks.verse:
शब्द कल्प मुपेक्ष्यापि वादयेत्स्वरमालिकाम्।
तानालापसमावेशम् बुद्ध्या कूर्याद् विचक्षणः।१४०।
blocks.text: Even setting aside the framing of words, one may play a svaramālikā (garland of notes); the discerning player should, with intelligence, bring in tānas and ālāpas.

The meaning is just this: a svaramālikā (garland of notes) is made even without words, on the basis of the mātrās of the tāla. Just as, on the basis of measure (weight), a sweet can be made even without grain, from milk and sugar alone, but with the addition of grain still finer sweets can be made, in the same way, if words are added, tāla and rāga are bound together easily. But at the time of playing, the words support the player indirectly.

When, by the rules above, a bandiś (composition) of some rāga has been made in some tāla, then to perform it one should bring into it various kinds of tānas in laya (tempo) and ālāpas bound in tāla, and play with absorption.

blocks.verse:
क्वविदर्धं क्वचिच्चांशम् पूर्णम् वावर्तनस्य च।
पूर्यते विविधैस्तानैः गतम् गीतम् च गायकैः।१४१।
blocks.text: Sometimes half, sometimes a part, or the whole of an āvartan: singers fill out the gat and the gīt with various tānas.

Taking one round of the tāla as one āvartan (cycle), a gat should be of at least one āvartan; but tānas are sometimes of half an āvartan, sometimes of a quarter of an āvartan, sometimes of three quarters, and so on. So after tānas of an incomplete āvartan, part of the gat is played to complete that āvartan; and sometimes also part of the gat is played to complete the āvartan by means of tihāīs. Tihāīs are of many kinds, from small to large. Their definition is given next.

blocks.verse:
त्रिरुक्तः स्वरसंघातः तृधायीति निगद्यते।
तानावसाने संयोज्यो मुख्यान्तश्च गुणान्वितः।१४२।
blocks.text: A cluster of notes said three times is called tṛdhāyī (tihāī); it is to be joined at the end of a tāna, should end on the main [note], and must have some quality.

That is, a group of notes used three times in a row is called a tihāī (a phrase played three times to land on sam); but the last note of that group should be the main sam note of the rāga, and the group must have a quality made by laya or a quality made by rāga. By quality made by laya is meant layakārī (rhythmic play), and by quality made by rāga is meant the rāga-identifying svara saṅgati (companionship of notes).

The tihāī belongs to tāla; it arises in the bols of the tabla. Most commonly 'dhā' is used at its end, e.g. - 'tiṭ dhā tiṭ dhā tiṭ dhā' and so on. These bols contain three dhās, so its correct name is (tridhāyī), whose corrupted form is known as (tihāī). If the sam is likened to a temple, we liken the tihāīs to the three steps that lead into the temple. Just as the third dhā comes to rest on the sam, so the third step comes to rest in the temple. Now the many kinds of tihāī are considered.

blocks.verse:
आहतोऽनाहतश्चैव तथाऽतीतश्च कथ्यते।
अविरामी विरामीति त्रिघायी बहुधा भवेत्।१४३।
blocks.text: The tihāī is said to be āhat, anāhat and atīt, and without pauses or with pauses; thus it is of many kinds.

That is, with the last syllable of some tihāīs the sam note is struck at once (on the first mātrā); and the last syllable of some tihāīs falls ahead of or behind the sam - these are called atīt (landing after sam) and anāghāt (landing off sam). Some tihāīs have more pause, some little pause, and in some there is no pause at all. In this way there are many tihāīs. Tihāīs that take more than one āvartan are called cakkardār tihāīs. If tihāīs are shorter than one āvartan, they are used in the second half of the tāla, so that the duty of reaching the sam can be fulfilled. Now, if you try to make tihāīs from three mātrās up to 16 mātrās in the form of notes, words and tāla bols, attend to the following points.

blocks.verse:
त्रिधायिनस्तु द्वौ भागौ कल्प्येते निर्मिमिषया।
आद्यस्तु गुणितो नित्यम् द्वितीयस्तु समस्वरः।१४४।
blocks.text: When one wishes to make a tihāī, two parts are devised: the first is always multiplied [in speed], and the second is the sam note.

That is, any tihāī can be divided into two parts, of which the first part has tempos such as double speed (it is multiplied), and the second part is filled with the sam note and the desired mātrās of pause; e.g. tabla bols such as tiṭ dhā, katiṭ dhā and tirakiṭ dhā, whose rendering in notes is SaRe Ga, NiSaRe Ga and ḌhaṆiSaRe Ga and so on; and if we render them in words, they could be kuch de [give something], tanik deṃ [give a little] and so on. In all these tihāīs the first part is multiplied in double, triple and quadruple speed (do gun, tīn gun and caugun) respectively, and the second part is filled by just one single syllable.

Now, if we wish to use these tihāīs in some tāla, we shall have to begin six mātrās before the sam, or, leaving out the sam, five mātrās before; and this will succeed fully only when the bansī player practises his tāla-bound gat sitting beside a player of a rhythm instrument. Here the melody player (svara vādaka) and the rhythm player (tāla vādaka) will be each other's partners. The melody player will have to understand the rhythm player's language; only then will he get the indication of the sam, that is, the first mātrā of the tāla. When the melody player wants to bring off one of his tihāīs, the rhythm player will not play any tihāī of his own but will keep playing the plain ṭhekā (the tāla's basic stroke pattern) clearly; and when the rhythm player wants to bring off one of his tihāīs, the melody player will hold back his tihāī and keep playing the plain gat. Once they have mastered this, both can also use tihāīs together.

blocks.verse:
मात्रेकयोगात् पूर्वस्मिन् परिणामस्त्रि मात्रिकः।
मात्रैकादपरस्मिन् तु परिणामों द्विमात्रिकः।१४५।
blocks.text: Adding one mātrā to the first part results in three mātrās; adding one mātrā to the second part results in two mātrās.

That is, if a group of one mātrā is added to the first part of a tihāī, then by the time the tihāī ends [three mātrās will have been added; and if] a pause of [one] mātrā is added [to the second part], the whole tihāī will grow by two mātrās. On the basis of these two actions you can make a tihāī of as many mātrās as you wish. For example, if in place of tiṭ dhā we make it tiṭ-tiṭ dhā, the whole tihāī will be of (9) mātrās, in which the ninth mātrā will fall on the sam; and if we make it tiṭ dhā –, it will come to only eight mātrās.
